title: How Futurology Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore futurology (futurism), the practice of recognizing and assessing potential future events. They cover its post-WWII origins in US military technological forecasting, Theodore von Karman's Air Force report, the RAND Corporation and the Delphi technique, Herman Kahn and scenario building and backcasting, the 1967 book The Year 2000, the Club of Rome and Limits to Growth, business forecasting at Royal Dutch Shell, Moore's law, Alvin Toffler's Future Shock, and science fiction predictions by Jules Verne, H.G. Wells, and Hugo Gernsback, plus a list of failed predictions. The episode ends with listener mail from Shelby about the hemophilia clotting factor and the HIV/AIDS crisis.

segments.title: Opening and sponsor read
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Squarespace, then Josh and Chuck introduce the topic of futurology and its mix of serious forecasting and speculative guessing.

segments.title: Futurology versus science fiction
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how futurologists differ from sci fi writers, with logic versus imagination, and how the era and culture shape predictions.

segments.title: Post-war origins of technological forecasting
segments.summary: Futurology became meaningful after World War Two when the US Air Force, under Hap Arnold, began forecasting technology. Theodore von Karman led a team that predicted drones, target-seeking missiles, supersonic aircraft, and the atom bomb.

segments.title: RAND and the Delphi technique
segments.summary: The RAND Corporation developed the Delphi technique for reaching expert consensus through anonymous, repeated questionnaires, illustrated by the Navy's search for a lost submarine.

segments.title: Scenarios, backcasting, and Herman Kahn
segments.summary: A scenario is defined as a detailed plausible future; backcasting works backward from a future state. Herman Kahn, who coined the term scenario in this context, wrote On Thermonuclear War and later founded the Hudson Institute.

segments.title: The Year 2000 and predictions of innovation
segments.summary: Kahn's 1967 book The Year 2000 argued that American capitalism could invent its way out of problems, listing one hundred predicted innovations such as lasers, new materials, birth control, nuclear power, and home computers.

segments.title: Club of Rome and Limits to Growth
segments.summary: The Club of Rome took a gloomy view on resource depletion and overpopulation. Its 1972 book Limits to Growth used computer models; the hosts note it is often misread as predicting civilizational collapse and that predictions of doom have often been wrong.

segments.title: Business forecasting, game theory, and Moore's law
segments.summary: Royal Dutch Shell adopted scenario planning for business. Game theory, disruptive technology, and the limits of prediction are discussed, along with Moore's law and Kahn's miss on the 1973 oil crisis.

segments.title: Future Shock and sci-fi predictions
segments.summary: Alvin Toffler's 1970 Future Shock predicted stress from rapid change. The hosts then discuss sci-fi writers who predicted events, including Jules Verne's Moon launch from Florida, H.G. Wells's tanks and atomic bomb, and Hugo Gernsback's Ralph 124C 41+.

segments.title: Failed predictions
segments.summary: A list of predictions that missed, including missile freight delivery, dissolving dishes, Canada under a dome, babies grown in labs, and personal helicopters.

segments.title: Listener mail from Shelby on HIV/AIDS and hemophilia
segments.summary: Shelby writes that the HIV/AIDS episode omitted the clotting factor concentrate story and the pharmaceutical industry's delay in pasteurizing it, and recommends the documentary Bad Blood.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and contact information and sign off.
